title_en: Fragments on the First Letter to the Corinthians
author: Didymus the Blind
addressee: Christian readers, especially those troubled by doubts about the resurrection
occasion: Didymus comments on 1 Corinthians 15–16 to refute those in Corinth who said the soul is perishable and bodily resurrection superfluous, and later heretics such as Marcionites, those who say only the soul is made alive, and those who posit a fifth substance.
argument: Paul wrote 1 Corinthians 15 to correct Corinthians who said the soul is perishable and the resurrection of the body is superfluous. Didymus argues that Christ truly died and rose in the body, and that his resurrection guarantees the resurrection of all people. He explains that the risen body is not the same perishable, soulish body that was sown, but a spiritual, incorruptible body transformed by God's power. He also refutes Marcionites who baptize the living for the dead, and heretics who say only the soul of the righteous is made alive in Christ. He closes by explaining Paul's practical instructions about the collection, Timothy, Apollos, and greetings.

outline.move: Didymus introduces Paul's purpose in 1 Corinthians 15: to refute those in Corinth who denied the soul's immortality and the resurrection of the body, and he explains that Christ's death and resurrection according to the Scriptures guarantee the resurrection of all.

Didymus explains Christ's reign and the subjection of enemies including death, addresses Greek mythological objections about gods who kill their fathers, refutes Marcionite baptismal practice, and notes Paul's sufferings as proof the resurrection is not vain.

Didymus expounds the difference between the soulish body that is sown and the spiritual body that is raised, insisting that the risen body is incorruptible by God's grace, not a fifth substance, and that only the righteous are changed, with discussion of alternative interpretations about who 'the dead' and 'we' are.

Didymus comments on Paul's closing instructions in 1 Corinthians 16: the collection on the first day of the week, Paul's stay in Ephesus, Timothy's visit, Apollos's delay, steadfastness in faith, and the final greeting and curse.

cast.name: Paul
cast.who: The apostle who wrote 1 Corinthians and whose teaching Didymus expounds.

cast.name: Christ
cast.who: The Savior whose death and resurrection guarantee the resurrection of all.

cast.name: Adam
cast.who: The first man, through whose transgression death entered; contrasted with Christ.

cast.name: Timothy
cast.who: Paul's fellow worker, sent to the Corinthians.

cast.name: Apollos
cast.who: Described by Didymus as having been bishop of Corinth, who withdrew from them because of the divisions among them, and was with Paul when urged but did not travel with the letter because it was not his will.

cast.name: Stephanas
cast.who: A Corinthian believer mentioned with Fortunatus and Achaicus.

cast.name: Fortunatus
cast.who: A Corinthian believer who, with Achaicus, supplied what was lacking.

cast.name: Achaicus
cast.who: A Corinthian believer who, with Fortunatus, supplied what was lacking.

cast.name: Origen
cast.who: Earlier Christian teacher cited by Didymus on the distinction between soul and spirit.

cast.name: Marcionites
cast.who: Heretics who baptized living people on behalf of the unbaptized dead.

voices.speaker: Paul
voices.how_marked: Quotations from 1 Corinthians, often introduced by φησίν or given as lemmata

voices.speaker: Heretics, doubters, and alternative exegetes
voices.how_marked: Introduced by phrases such as τινὲς λέγουσι, οἱ ἀπατῶντες, or indirect discourse, including some who offer alternative interpretations of 1 Cor 15:51-52

key_terms.sense: The rising of the dead, especially the bodily resurrection guaranteed by Christ's resurrection.
The rational soul, which Didymus insists is immortal and distinct from the body.
The body as sown in this present life, animated by the soul and subject to corruption, weakness, and dishonor.
The risen body transformed by the Holy Spirit, incorruptible, powerful, and glorious.
Incorruptibility of the risen body, given by God's grace, not an inherent fifth substance.
Firstfruits; Christ as the first of the risen dead, and the Stephanas household as first believers or leaders in service.
Death as the last enemy destroyed by Christ, and the state from which the dead are raised.
Christ's reign over those being saved, culminating in the subjection of all enemies and the handing over of the kingdom to the Father.
The Holy Spirit, or the higher part of a holy person, distinguished from the soul and associated with virtue.
The change of the righteous at the resurrection, from glory to glory, in soul and body.
The hidden truth about the resurrection that Paul reveals to the Corinthians.
Victory, used by Paul for death's apparent triumph, which is swallowed up by immortality.
The sting of death, identified with sin, by which death wounds people.
The Christian assemblies in the Roman province of Asia who send greetings to Corinth.

scripture: Didymus follows the Septuagint (LXX) for Old Testament quotations and numbering. He cites Hosea for the phrase rendered by Paul as 'victory' instead of 'justice' (Hosea 13:14 LXX). Psalm numbering follows the LXX. Modern citations should use standard English Bible names and numbering, noting LXX differences where relevant.
uncertain: The exact date of composition within Didymus's lifetime.
Whether the fragments preserve Didymus's original wording or are catena excerpts.
The precise identity of the 'some' who held various opinions about the resurrection and the change.
The reading of the variant in 1 Corinthians 15:51 that Didymus discusses.

_unresolved_facts.claim: and later heretics such as Marcionites, those who say only the soul is made alive, and those who posit a fifth substance
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ὅταν δὲ λέγωμεν σῶμα ἄφθαρτον, οὐ πέμπτην οὐσίαν λέγομεν, ὥς τινες περὶ τῶν ἄστρων ὑπενόησαν
_unresolved_facts.fix: Didymus mentions those who posit a fifth substance (πέμπτην οὐσίαν) in the context of explaining what the incorruptible body is NOT, not as part of the original Corinthian opponents. These are astronomers/philosophers (περὶ τῶν ἄστρων), not heretics opposing resurrection. The occasion should distinguish: (1) original Corinthians denying soul's immortality and bodily resurrection, (2) Marcionites, (3) heretics saying only the soul of the righteous is made alive, and (4) philosophers positing a fifth substance for heavenly bodies.

_unresolved_facts.claim: He also refutes Marcionites who baptize the living for the dead
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Οἱ ἀπὸ Μαρκίωνος ἀντὶ ἀφωτίστων τεθνεώτων βαπτίζουσι ζῶντας
_unresolved_facts.fix: He refutes Marcionites who baptize living people ON BEHALF OF the unbaptized dead (ἀντὶ ἀφωτίστων τεθνεώτων), not 'the living for the dead' as a vague phrase. The key point is substitutionary baptism for unbaptized dead persons, not merely 'living for dead' generally.

_unresolved_facts.claim: addresses Greek mythological objections about gods who kill their fathers
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Πρός τε τὴν Ἑλλήνων μυθολογίαν τε καὶ ἀπάτην εἰρῆσθαι ταῦτα εἰπόντες τῶν φασκόντων πατραλοίας εἶναι θεούς
_unresolved_facts.fix: Didymus says these things were spoken 'πρὸς τὴν Ἑλλήνων μυθολογίαν τε καὶ ἀπάτην' (against Greek mythology and deception) 'τῶν φασκόντων πατραλοίας εἶναι θεούς' (of those saying there are gods who kill their fathers). The outline should note this is about gods who are 'patraloias' (father-killers), not merely 'objections about' such gods—it's a specific charge against Greek mythological theology in relation to Christ's subjection to the Father.

_unresolved_facts.claim: and notes Paul's sufferings as proof the resurrection is not vain
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Ὅσον κατ' ἀνθρώπινον ἧκε λογισμόν, ἐθηριομάχησα ἐν Ἐφέσῳ ἐγὼ οὐκ ἂν ὑποστῆναι τοῦτο βουληθεὶς ὑπὲρ τῆς ἀληθείας, εἰ–νεκροὶ οὐκ ἐγείρονται
_unresolved_facts.fix: Didymus presents this as Paul speaking in first person about his own willingness to face beasts at Ephesus—'I would not have been willing to endure this for the truth if the dead are not raised.' The outline should clarify this is Paul's autobiographical argument, not Didymus 'noting' Paul's sufferings as external proof.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Described by Didymus as having been bishop of Corinth
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Ἐπειδὴ ὁ Ἀπολλῶς ἐπίσκοπος ἦν Κορίνθου
_unresolved_facts.fix: The source does say this (ἐπίσκοπος ἦν Κορίνθου), so this is actually supported. No problem.

_unresolved_facts.claim: who withdrew from them because of the divisions among them
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ἀπέστη ἐξ αὐτῶν διὰ τὰ ἐν αὐτοῖς σχίσματα
_unresolved_facts.fix: The source says ἀπέστη ἐξ αὐτῶν (he stood away/departed from them), which is stronger than 'withdrew'—it implies he left them, abandoned them, or separated from them due to the schisms. 'Withdrew' is too neutral; 'departed from them' or 'left them' is more accurate.

_unresolved_facts.claim: and was with Paul when urged but did not travel with the letter because it was not his will
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: καὶ νῦν παρακληθεὶς οὐ συνεξεδήμησε τῇ ἐπιστολῇ... ὅτι οὐκ ἦν θέλημα
_unresolved_facts.fix: The source says οὐ συνεξεδήμησε τῇ ἐπιστολῇ (he did not travel out together with the letter), not merely 'did not travel with the letter.' More importantly, οὐκ ἦν θέλημα means 'it was not [his] will' or 'it was not [God's] will'—the subject is ambiguous. The brief assumes it's Apollos's will, but it could be God's will. Should say 'because it was not the will' or note the ambiguity.

_unresolved_facts.claim: including some who offer alternative interpretations of 1 Cor 15:51-52
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: τινὲς δὲ λέγουσιν ὧδε τὸ ἡ μεῖς ἀλλαγησόμεθα ἀντὶ τοῦ οἷα ἄλλοι τινὲς ὄντες παρὰ τοὺς νεκρούς... ἄλλος δέ φησι τοὺς ἁμαρτωλοὺς εἶναι τοὺς νεκρούς
_unresolved_facts.fix: The source presents multiple specific alternative interpretations: (1) some (τινὲς) say 'we will be changed' means 'as others different from the dead,' with bodies raised incorruptible while souls are changed to a better quality; (2) another (ἄλλος) says the dead are sinners who are raised incorruptible to endure eternal punishments, while those changed from glory to glory are those who lived virtuously. The brief oversimplifies by saying 'some who offer alternative interpretations' without noting these are specific named exegetes with distinct views.
No psalms are cited in the source text. The only OT citation is Hosea (Ὠσηὲ). This claim about Psalm numbering is unsupported by the provided source.
